eras.name: Bronze Age and Troy
eras.kicker: The palaces were a supply chain
eras.pull: Copper, tin, grain, and timber had to meet. When the meetings stopped, the palace system stopped with them.

figure.label: The eastern palace network breaks
figure.caveat: A generation of collapse, not a single dated battle.

eras.imageAlt: A Bronze Age galley beside a stone quay at dusk, copper ingots on the dock and a citadel on the hill behind.
narrative: Before anyone drew a map of the Mediterranean, the sea was already a metals market. Cyprus had the copper. Tin came from farther off, probably the west and the Anatolian hinterland. Cedar came from the Lebanon. Grain, oil, wine, and dyed cloth moved the other way. Palaces at Mycenae, Knossos, Hattusa, and Ugarit did not float on tribute alone. They floated on ships that could keep those goods in the same ledger.

The Uluburun wreck, off the Lycian coast around 1300 BCE, is the ledger recovered. Oxhide copper ingots, tin, glass, ebony, resin, and Canaanite jars sat in one hull. A single ship was already a multi-basin venture. The wreck is one voyage. The pattern is the point: the eastern sea was a connected workshop, and the workshop's inventory was heavy.

Troy sits on that story because of where it sits. The Dardanelles are the door between the Aegean and the Black Sea, and the current there is a weapon. Whoever held the Asian shore could tax, pilot, or refuse a hull. Later Greeks made a war of it. The archaeological city is a stack of destructions, not a script. Treat the Trojan War as a memory of a strait that mattered, not as a timetable.

Around 1200 BCE the letters stop. Ugarit writes that enemy ships have been seen, and then Ugarit goes quiet. Palaces burn or empty from the Peloponnese to the Levant. The cause was not one fleet of 'Sea Peoples' in the Victorian sense. Drought, earthquake, migration, and the brittleness of palace credit all have evidence behind them. The maritime fact is simpler. A network priced for good years could not reroute when several coasts failed at once.

eras.name: Phoenicians and Greek colonisation
eras.kicker: The sea fills in with cities
eras.pull: Colonisation was a trade policy that planted people. The western basin stops being a rumor.

figure.label: Carthage's traditional founding date
figure.caveat: A classical tradition, not an excavation date. The city is real; the year is a convention.

eras.imageAlt: A Phoenician bireme leaving a Levantine stone harbor at dusk.
narrative: After the collapse, the survivors who could still build ships were not the inland palaces. They were coastal cities with timber, dye, and a habit of going to sea. Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos turned the Levantine run into a commercial specialty. Their colonies and waystations reached Cyprus, North Africa, western Sicily, Sardinia, and, beyond the strait, Gades. The western Mediterranean enters the written maritime world from the east, carried by Phoenician hulls.

Greek-speaking towns did the same thing on a different coast. From the eighth century, Euboeans, Corinthians, Achaeans, and others planted cities in Sicily, southern Italy, the Adriatic, Cyrenaica, and as far as Massalia. This was not a state plan. It was land hunger, factional exile, metal hunger, and a merchant's map, repeated until the coasts spoke Greek. Syracuse, Taras, Cyrene, and Massalia are the durable results.

The two networks met in the middle of the sea and did not merge. Sicily becomes the argument. Phoenician and then Carthaginian towns hold the west of the island. Greek towns hold the east. The Sicily Channel is no longer empty water. It is a border between commercial systems, and borders on the water are where the next century's wars will be fought.

Two quiet inventions matter more than any single colony. The bireme and, late in the period, the trireme turn the oared ship into a weapon with a ram. And in Lydia and the Greek cities, coinage appears. A cargo can now be priced in a unit that is not a sack of grain. Maritime credit, in the later Athenian sense, is still ahead. The precondition, a portable standard of value, is here.

eras.name: Persian wars to Alexander
eras.kicker: A navy becomes a fiscal system
eras.pull: Athens turned Black Sea grain, a silver mine, and a strait into a tribute empire. The bill was a trireme.

figure.label: Salamis. The trireme fleet decides a war
figure.caveat: A dated battle. The fiscal system around it lasts longer than the victory.

eras.imageAlt: Greek triremes in a narrow strait at dawn, oars in the water and rocky headlands in the haze.
narrative: Persia was a land empire that learned the sea by hiring it. Phoenician and Ionian squadrons carried the great kings toward Greece. Athens answered with a crash naval program, funded by the silver of Laurion and manned by citizens who would later expect a political return. Salamis in 480 BCE is the famous day. The structural fact is the 200 triremes: a city-state had capitalized a fleet the way a later state would capitalize a dockyard.

The Delian League starts as an anti-Persian alliance and becomes an Athenian revenue system. Allies pay ships or, more conveniently, silver. The silver builds more Athenian ships. Grain from the Black Sea, especially the Bosporan kingdom, feeds the city that can no longer feed itself. The Dardanelles and the Bosporus stop being geography and become the throat of Athenian policy. When Sparta cuts that throat at Aegospotami in 405, the empire ends in a season.

The fourth century invents the paperwork. Athenian court speeches, above all the maritime cases later filed under Demosthenes, show bottomry loans: money advanced on a hull and cargo, repayable only if the ship arrives, at a rate that prices the risk. This is not yet the Italian commenda, but it is maritime finance in the open. A lender in Piraeus is underwriting a voyage to the Pontus.

Alexander does not win a great naval war. He removes the Persian fleet's bases. Tyre falls in 332 after a siege that is really a harbor engineering project. Egypt falls the same year, and Alexandria is founded on a site chosen because it can be a port. The Hellenistic kingdoms that follow, Ptolemaic Egypt especially, inherit the grain, the timber problem, and the need for a royal navy. The Roman republic is about to walk into a sea these kingdoms already organized.

eras.name: Carthage and Rome
eras.kicker: Mare Nostrum is a grain administration
eras.pull: Rome did not love the sea. It taxed it, policed it, and fed a million people from it.

figure.label: Carthage and Corinth destroyed in one year
figure.caveat: The political horizon clears. The grain problem does not.

eras.imageAlt: A Roman grain ship approaching a harbor lighthouse in the evening, amphorae stacked on the quay.
narrative: Rome enters the water as a land power that has run out of land enemies on its own peninsula. The first war with Carthage, from 264 BCE, is a war about Sicily and about who is allowed to float there. Rome copies the other side's ships, loses fleets to weather, and learns that a navy is a timber and training problem. By the end of the third war, in 146, there is no second naval system in the west. Corinth is removed the same year. The sea has one sheriff, and the sheriff would rather be a road.

The republic's real maritime crisis is piracy. With the Hellenistic navies gone and the republic unwilling to pay for a standing fleet, raiders professionalize. In 67 BCE Pompey is given an extraordinary command and sweeps them in a season, which proves that the problem was budget and jurisdiction, not mystery. The empire then does the boring version: harbors, patrols, and a legal climate in which a cargo can be insured by contract.

The cargo that justifies all of it is Egyptian grain. The annona, the state grain supply, moves from Alexandria to Puteoli and then to Portus, the harbor Claudius and Trajan build because Ostia silts and Rome cannot gamble the harvest on a river mouth. A delay is a riot. Maritime logistics becomes urban policy. North African grain joins Egyptian grain as the city's second lung.

Roman private trade is wider than the annona. Wine, oil, garum, marble, glass, and enslaved people move in amphorae and hulls whose wrecks still line the French and Italian coasts. The Red Sea ports, Berenike above all, reach into the Indian Ocean monsoon trade. Pepper arrives. The money that pays for it, silver and gold coin, worries Pliny. None of this requires a sea-level canal. A desert road from the Nile to a Red Sea beach is enough, which is why Suez is not yet a strait and is already a corridor.

In 476 the last western emperor is retired. The eastern empire, taxed from Constantinople, still has the ships, the grain, and the strait. Calling the whole period 'Rome' hides that handoff. It should not hide the achievement. For half a millennium one legal and naval order made a million-person city a coastal fact.

eras.pull: Egypt's grain had fed the old Rome. After 642 it fed a different empire, and Constantinople had to live on a smaller sea.

eras.imageAlt: A medieval dromon on dark water in front of the sea walls of Constantinople.
narrative: The eastern Roman state survives because it keeps the strait and a fleet. Justinian's reconquest, in the sixth century, takes back Carthage and, for a while, Italy, using the sea as a road the Goths and Vandals cannot reliably cut. It is expensive. Plague and Persian war then shrink the base. When Arab armies take Syria in the 630s and Egypt by 642, the empire loses the provinces that had paid for the navy and filled the granaries. The capital does not fall. Its diet changes.

Two sieges of Constantinople, in 674–678 and 717–718, are maritime events even though the walls are the picture everyone remembers. An Arab fleet in the Marmara is an attempt to close the city's own door. Greek fire, the empire's napalm, is a strait weapon: it matters most in narrow water where a slower fleet cannot scatter. The caliphate remains a great naval power anyway. From Syria and then from Kairouan and Tunis it takes Cyprus as a condominium, raids the islands, and between 827 and 902 conquers Sicily.

Trade does not stop because the frontier is hostile. It changes brokers. Jewish, Syrian, and then Muslim merchants move goods the palaces no longer move as tribute. Amalfi, Gaeta, and Venice appear in the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian gaps as Latin towns that can sell to both sides. Venice is still legally a Byzantine backwater. In practice it is learning the carrying trade that will later embarrass its overlord.

The Red Sea and the Gulf go the other way. With Egypt and Syria inside the caliphate, Indian Ocean goods come up the Red Sea to a Muslim Egypt and across the isthmus, or up the Gulf to Basra and Baghdad. Hormuz is not yet the famous kingdom. The corridor is. The Mediterranean is no longer the only rich sea attached to this map, and it is no longer one legal world. Two fiscal systems face each other across a water both of them can cross and neither of them can close.

eras.kicker: The contract is the new harbor
eras.pull: A merchant republic could rent a crusade, own a quarter of a foreign city, and insure the voyage that paid for both.

eras.imageAlt: A medieval merchant galley in a foggy arsenal basin, timber sheds and lantern light.
narrative: By the eleventh century the carrying trade has names, fleets, and lawyers. Venice, Genoa, and Pisa are not empires with incidental ships. They are ship-owning cities. The First Crusade and its successors give them what they actually want, which is not Jerusalem. It is a chain of fondachi, exempt quarters with a church, a warehouse, an oven, and a legal privilege, from the Adriatic to the Levant. Acre, Tyre, and later Famagusta are nodes in a Latin commercial net laid over a Muslim and Greek sea.

Venetian practice turns risk into a repeatable instrument. The colleganza, a local form of the commenda, splits a voyage between a staying investor and a travelling partner. Convoys, the muda, sail on a calendar to Romania and to the Levant. The state builds the Arsenal, a dockyard that can lay down hulls in series, and it forces nobles onto the galleys so that trade and defense are the same social class. Genoa answers with credit, colonies in the Black Sea, and a talent for private violence. The two cities fight each other as often as they fight anyone else.

The Black Sea opens wide after 1204, and wider again once the Mongol peace makes the roads behind Tana and Caffa usable. Grain, hides, enslaved people, and alum move from the Pontus into Italian hulls. Caffa, on the Crimean coast, is a Genoese city on someone else's horizon. This is the grain and labor market Athens once reached by diplomacy. It is now reached by colony. The plague of the mid-fourteenth century will travel the same pontoon of ships.

Spice still comes through Egypt. The Karimi merchants and the Mamluk customs house at Alexandria are the tollgate of the Indian Ocean, reached via the Red Sea and the isthmus. No Christian fleet holds Bab el-Mandeb. They pay, or they try the Gulf, where the kingdom of Hormuz is the entrepot, and then a caravan. The Atlantic is not yet the bypass. It is about to be. In 1453 the Ottoman gun on the Bosporus ends the Roman capital the Italian cities had been exploiting for two centuries. The contracts survive. The political weather does not.

eras.imageAlt: Sixteenth-century galleys in a long line on a dark sea at sunset, smoke low on the water.
narrative: After 1453 the Bosporus is an Ottoman city and the Dardanelles are an Ottoman door. Selim takes Syria and Egypt in 1516–1517, which means the spice isthmus, the Red Sea, and the two holy cities' maritime approaches change hands together. The empire is now a three-sea state: Black Sea grain, Mediterranean galleys, and a Red Sea it has to defend against the Portuguese. Bab el-Mandeb and Aden become frontier posts. Hormuz, taken by the Portuguese in 1515, is the Gulf post the Ottomans do not get. An English-Persian force takes it back for the Safavids in 1622.

Lepanto, on 7 October 1571, is the largest galley battle of the age. The Holy League, Habsburg Spain and Venice foremost, destroys an Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras. It is a real victory and a bad prophecy. Hulls were the expendable part. Crews and credit were not, and the sultan's dockyards replaced the hulls. Venice loses Cyprus anyway. The galley remains the Mediterranean warship because the wind is unreliable and the coasts are close. It is no longer the ship that sets the world price of pepper.

Vasco da Gama's arrival in India in 1498 does that. Spice that can round the Cape does not have to pay the Mamluk and then the Ottoman and then the Venetian. It still does, for a long time, because the old route is organized and the new one is violent. But the monopoly is gone. The Mediterranean becomes, in Braudel's sense, a sea of short distances and stubborn structures: grain, wool, silk, currants, and a carrying trade increasingly done by Dutch, English, and French sails. The Levant Company and the port of Livorno, a deliberately tolerant free port, are the new institutions. Izmir rises as the Anatolian export town.

Security is a corsair industry. The Barbary regencies of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, nominally Ottoman, run a raiding economy against Christian coasts and ships, financed by ransom and by the sale of captives. The Knights of Malta and the Tuscan galleys do the mirror-image business. Captivity is a Mediterranean institution, with consuls, redemptionist priests, and price lists. It is also a migration, forced and in both directions across the religious line.

The money is no longer only Venetian. Genoese bankers fund the Spanish crown. Bills of exchange clear at the fairs of Besançon and Piacenza. Maritime insurance is a priced contract in Venice, Genoa, and then Amsterdam, which is not a Mediterranean city and nevertheless sets the rate. Karlowitz, in 1699, marks the Ottoman land retreat in Europe. The sea arrangement, Ottoman straits and Habsburg Spain's western basin, is already older than that treaty and about to be rewritten by sail, Russia, and a canal that does not exist yet.

eras.imageAlt: A nineteenth-century steamship with a coal plume moving through the Suez Canal between desert banks.
narrative: The eighteenth century still looks like sail and corsairs. The Barbary regencies keep raiding until the early nineteenth century, when European and American naval expeditions, and then the French conquest of Algiers in 1830, close the business. Russia reaches the Black Sea for good, founds Sevastopol, and after the 1829 Treaty of Adrianople turns Odessa into a wheat port for Europe. Greek independence, between 1821 and 1830, is a maritime war as much as a land one. None of this yet changes the shape of the map. The Cape is still the way to India.

Steam and Egypt change the shape. A reliable schedule needs coal, and coal needs depots. Gibraltar, Malta, Port Said, and Aden become a chain of British bunkers. The submarine telegraph, Malta to Alexandria in the 1860s, puts naval orders on a wire that follows the same chain. The canal itself, cut by a French company under Ferdinand de Lesseps and opened in 1869, is only 164 kilometers and politically enormous. It joins the Mediterranean to the Red Sea at sea level. Bab el-Mandeb stops being a spice-coast anecdote and becomes the second half of the same door.

The finance is ugly and modern. Egypt borrows in European markets to look like a nineteenth-century state and to pay for the canal's world. By 1875 the khedive sells his shares to the British government. By 1876 Egyptian finances are under international control. By 1882 Britain occupies the country. A waterway built as a commercial concession becomes the security core of an empire that did not dig it. French capital, British occupation, Ottoman sovereignty on paper, and Egyptian debt: four layers on one ditch.

The Black Sea grain trade and the canal trade are the two new economic facts, and they pull in opposite directions. Odessa wheat goes out through the straits toward Marseille and London. Indian and East Asian goods come in through Suez toward Trieste, Genoa, and Marseille, which revive as liner ports. Trieste is Austria's bid to be a maritime power. The Ottoman Empire, the legal owner of the straits, is handled by treaty. The 1841 London Straits Convention closes the Dardanelles and Bosporus to foreign warships in peacetime. Russia hates the constraint. Britain depends on it. The Crimean War, 1853–1856, is what happens when the constraint fails.

On the Gulf side, the same empire that bunkers Aden signs the trucial arrangements that put the Arab side of Hormuz under British maritime protection. Oil is not yet the cargo. Pearls, dates, and the mail steamer are. The cargo is about to change. Abadan's refinery opens in 1913, one year before the war that will teach every admiralty what a fuel tanker is for.

basins.text: France takes Algiers in 1830 and spends the century turning a corsair coast into a settler colony. Spain holds the Moroccan shore's attention and never stops claiming Gibraltar. Marseille becomes a liner port. The western strait is British, and the traffic through it is everybody's.

basins.name: Central Mediterranean
basins.states: Italy, Malta, Tunisia, Sicily
basins.text: Italian unification puts a new state on both sides of the Sicily Channel. Malta is the British dockyard in the middle. France occupies Tunisia in 1881. The channel is no longer a galley border. It is a passage between coal piles.

basins.name: Adriatic
basins.states: Austria-Hungary, the Italian shore, the Ottoman Balkans
basins.text: Trieste is the bet. Austria tries to turn a deep harbor into a share of the canal trade. Venice is a memory with a port. The eastern Adriatic is still Ottoman until the century's crises start pulling it loose.

basins.name: Eastern Mediterranean
basins.states: Ottoman Empire, Egypt, Greece
basins.text: Greece is independent and irredentist. The Ottoman state is sovereign and supervised. Egypt is the special case: formally Ottoman, financially European, militarily British after 1882. Cyprus passes to British administration in 1878.

basins.name: Black Sea
basins.states: Russia, the Ottoman straits, Romania, Bulgaria
basins.text: Odessa grain is the economic fact. The straits conventions are the legal fact. Romania and Bulgaria emerge as coastal states out of Ottoman retreat. Sevastopol's destruction in the Crimean War is a reminder that a grain sea is also a fleet sea.

basins.name: Red Sea, Suez, and the Gulf
basins.states: Egypt, Aden, the Trucial coast, Persia
basins.text: One route, three legal regimes. Egypt hosts the canal and loses control of it. Aden watches Bab el-Mandeb. The Arab side of Hormuz is under British maritime treaties, and Persia has Abadan. Oil is a footnote in 1913 and the plot of the next chapter.

eras.name: World wars and the coming of oil
eras.kicker: The sea as a ration and a mandate
eras.pull: Two wars turned convoys into a way of life, replaced coal with oil, and left the straits under a treaty Turkey still administers.

figure.label: Montreux. Turkey keeps the keys to the straits
figure.caveat: A regime written between the wars and still the operating law.

eras.imageAlt: A wartime convoy in silhouette on a dark Mediterranean night, merchant hulls and one escort.
narrative: The 1914 war reaches this sea immediately because the sea is the road to Russia and the road to India. The Dardanelles campaign of 1915 is an attempt to open a supply line to the Black Sea by force, and it fails on the hills above the strait it came to take. The Ottoman Empire closes the passage. Russia starves for shells it might have received by water. Gallipoli is remembered as a landing. It was a logistics argument about a strait.

Oil arrives as a strategic cargo during the same war and never leaves. The Royal Navy has begun to burn oil. Abadan matters. After 1918 the Ottoman Arab provinces are divided by mandate, not by the people living in them. San Remo in 1920 and the treaties that follow put Iraq's oil, the Palestine coast, and the Syrian ports into British and French administration. Pipelines are designed toward Haifa and Tripoli because a barrel that reaches a Mediterranean terminal skips the long Gulf passage. The states that will later nationalize this oil are being drawn, in London and Paris, as rectangles.

The interwar straits settlement is the piece that lasts. Lausanne in 1923 settles the Greek-Turkish war and includes a straits regime too loose for Turkey's comfort. Montreux in 1936 revises it. Turkey remilitarizes the straits and administers a detailed schedule of what kind of warship may pass, in peace and in war. Merchant traffic stays free. The Black Sea is not an open naval square. It is a lake with a doorman, and the doorman is a coastal state, not a London conference. That is the rule under which every later Black Sea war is conducted.

The second war in this sea is a convoy war. Malta has to be fed. The Axis tries to close the Sicily Channel from Africa and Sicily. Taranto in 1940 shows that aircraft can cripple a battle fleet in harbor. Crete in 1941 is taken from the air and costs the German airborne arm. Operation Pedestal in 1942 is a convoy fought through to Malta because the island is a runway and a harbor, not a symbol. North Africa changes hands by sea. Whoever cannot land fuel cannot hold the desert.

The human accounting is not a cargo table. The 1923 population exchange, agreed at Lausanne, moves more than a million people across the Aegean, Greek Orthodox from Anatolia and Muslims from Greece. Wartime famine in Greece, deportations, and the flight of Jewish communities from ports that had held them since the sixteenth century break the commercial cities the previous era built. In 1945 the canals and the oil are intact enough to matter. The old port societies are not.

basins.name: The straits
basins.states: Turkey, and everyone who needs the Black Sea
basins.text: Gallipoli fails. Lausanne disappoints Ankara. Montreux satisfies it. From 1936 the question is no longer whether the great powers will garrison the Bosporus. It is how Turkey reads the convention when the great powers are at war.

basins.name: Central Mediterranean
basins.states: Italy, Malta, Libya, Tunisia
basins.text: Italy's bid for a closed sea fails in convoy battles. Malta, supplied at enormous cost, is the unsinkable airfield. Libya is an Italian colony and then a battlefield. The Sicily Channel is the most expensive water of the war.

basins.name: Eastern Mediterranean
basins.states: Egypt, the Palestine mandate, Greece, Cyprus
basins.text: Alexandria is a fleet base. Greece is occupied and starved. The Palestine mandate receives both a pipeline and a refugee pressure Britain tries to restrict. Cyprus is a quiet British island that will not stay quiet.

basins.name: Levant mandates
basins.states: France in Syria and Lebanon, Britain in Iraq and Transjordan
basins.text: Ports and pipelines are run for the mandatory powers. Local politics are already national. The oil concession in Iraq is the economic constitution of a state that did not write it.

basins.name: Black Sea
basins.states: Soviet Union, Romania, Bulgaria, Turkey
basins.text: A war zone. Odessa and Sevastopol are shattered. Romanian oil at Ploiești is a strategic target. Neutral Turkey's reading of Montreux is the only reason the sea is not simply a Soviet-German duel with open doors.

basins.name: Gulf and Red Sea
basins.states: Iran, the Arabian shore, Aden
basins.text: Abadan is important enough to invade Iran for, in 1941, alongside the Soviet Union. The Red Sea is the back door to Suez and is kept open. Hormuz is quiet because Britain still polices the Gulf. The noise is underground, in the oilfields.

eras.name: Cold War, containers, and tankers
eras.kicker: The hull grows up, and the canal closes
eras.pull: Two superpower squadrons shared a sea while the cargo quietly changed from break-bulk and barrels to containers, and Suez spent eight years shut.

figure.label: Suez stays closed after the Six-Day War
figure.caveat: Eight years. Asia–Europe freight goes around the Cape, and the tanker gets larger because of it.

eras.imageAlt: A container ship and a tanker passing the Rock of Gibraltar at dusk.
narrative: The postwar settlement puts an American fleet in the Mediterranean and, from the late 1960s, a Soviet squadron to watch it. The Sixth Fleet and the Fifth Eskadra are the visible Cold War. They are not the economic story. The economic story is a hull that stops fitting the ports built for it, and a canal that closes.

Nasser nationalizes the canal company in 1956. Britain, France, and Israel attack. The United States and the Soviet Union, for different reasons, make them stop. The canal reopens under Egyptian sovereignty, which is the real result. In June 1967 it closes again with the Six-Day War and stays closed until 1975. Eight years of closure do three things. They put Asia–Europe trade back on the Cape. They justify a generation of very large crude carriers that would not have fit the canal anyway. And they teach shippers that a single ditch is an operational risk, not a law of nature.

The container does the quieter damage. Malcolm McLean's first container voyage is an American coastal trip in 1956. The Mediterranean adopts the box through the late 1960s and 1970s. A port is no longer a crowd of stevedores and a warehouse. It is a gantry crane, a yard, and a truck gate. Cities that cannot buy the crane lose the trade to cities that can. Labor on the waterfront collapses. The political economy of Marseille, Genoa, and Piraeus changes in a decade, and the change looks like technology rather than a decision.

Oil is the other bulk. Gulf production, the 1973 embargo, and the price shock move more money through this map than any spice convoy. The tankers load east of Hormuz and, while Suez is shut, go the long way. When the canal reopens it is too small for the biggest ships, so the Sumed pipeline from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean is built as a bypass for barrels. The Strait of Hormuz becomes what Bab el-Mandeb was in the spice age: the narrow place where a world price can be touched. The Iran–Iraq tanker war of the 1980s is the demonstration.

The human flow changes direction. Decolonization pulls settlers out of Algeria in 1962 and rearranges the rest of the Maghreb. Labor migration carries Maghrebi and later Turkish workers toward France and Germany. The 1974 war in Cyprus partitions an island that sits on the eastern routes. Palestinian displacement, from 1948 and again from 1967, remakes Gaza, Beirut, and Amman. None of this is a single maritime event. All of it passes through port cities and changes who they are for. The superpower squadrons sail past the result.

conflicts.name: Six-Day War closure

basins.name: Central Mediterranean
basins.states: Italy, Malta, Libya, Tunisia
basins.text: Malta becomes independent in 1964 and asks the fleets to thin out. Libya under Gaddafi turns an oil coast into a political actor and a port of call for the Soviet squadron. Italy's ports industrialize or decline by the crane, not by the admiral.

basins.name: Eastern Mediterranean
basins.states: Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, Israel, Egypt, Syria, Lebanon
basins.text: A crowded front. Arab-Israeli wars, the Lebanese civil war, the Cyprus division, and a Greek-Turkish relationship inside NATO that is also a maritime boundary dispute. Egypt's separate peace after 1978 splits the basin politically and reopens a commercial path.

basins.name: Black Sea
basins.states: Soviet Union, Romania, Bulgaria, Turkey
basins.text: A Warsaw Pact coast plus Turkey. Montreux keeps Western warships on a quota and Soviet exits on a rule. Commercial grain and a closed naval politics share the water. The Soviet hospital and repair ships in the Mediterranean start their voyages here.

basins.name: Suez and the Red Sea
basins.states: Egypt, Israel, Yemen, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia
basins.text: Closure is the fact that dominates. The Bab el-Mandeb end is part of the same problem: a blocked canal makes the Red Sea a dead end for the big trades. Reopening in 1975, and the Sumed line, put the corridor back without restoring the old monopoly.

basins.name: Gulf and Hormuz
basins.states: Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the smaller Arab states
basins.text: This is where the tonnage is. The 1973 embargo is a producer decision. The 1980s tanker war is an industrial war fought on hulls. A US escort regime in 1987–88 says out loud that the strait is a security interest of a state that does not border it.

eras.name: Cables, sanctions, and the straits
eras.kicker: The cargo is a container, a barrel, a grain ship, and a pulse of light
eras.pull: The same six doors still tax the world. What changed is that closing one of them is now a financial instrument, a naval task, and a software problem.

eras.imageAlt: A modern container ship at night on a dark strait, with a fiber-optic cable lying on the seabed below.
narrative: The post-1991 sea looks commercial until it does not. Container hubs reorganize the basin. Tanger Med, Algeciras, Valencia, Gioia Tauro, Marsaxlokk, Piraeus, and Port Said compete as transshipment machines rather than as doors to their own hinterlands. Piraeus is the clearest political example: a Greek port, a COSCO concession from 2009, and a controlling Chinese stake from 2016. A harbor can be inside the European customs union and inside a Chinese state company's network at the same time. Greek beneficial owners, meanwhile, remain among the largest private fleets in the world, flagged wherever the finance is cheapest. The owner, the flag, the cargo, and the terminal can be four different countries.

Suez is Egypt's toll booth and the route's single point of failure. The Ever Given grounding in March 2021 blocks the canal for six days and shows, in public, a queue measured in billions. From late 2023, attacks on shipping in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden divert a large share of Asia–Europe container traffic around the Cape. The diversion adds on the order of ten days and a fuel bill large enough to move freight rates, insurance premia, and European shelf prices. Egypt loses tolls. The Cape ports gain calls they did not ask to plan for. Bab el-Mandeb is doing nineteenth-century work with twenty-first-century insurance.

The Black Sea after February 2022 is a grain and sanctions story conducted under Montreux. Turkey closes the straits to the warships of the belligerents, which is what the convention is for, and the decision matters as much as any fleet movement. Ukraine's ports are mined, blockaded, and struck. The Black Sea Grain Initiative, July 2022 to July 2023, is a negotiated corridor for food, brokered with the United Nations and Turkey, and it does not survive. Grain still moves afterward by coastal and river workarounds and at a war premium. A shadow fleet of older tankers, opaque ownership, and weak insurance carries sanctioned oil through the same legal geography. The price cap is a financial rule. The strait is where it either holds or leaks.

Under the hulls is the other network. Fiber-optic systems, SEA-ME-WE, AAE-1, and newer cables such as 2Africa and Blue Raman among them, land on these coasts and cross the same narrows as the ships. The lines drawn on this map are schematic corridors, not the cables' real positions. The strategic fact does not require the coordinates. A cut or a fault in a congested corridor is a financial outage and a political temptation, and attribution is slow. Alongside the glass, East Mediterranean gas, Leviathan, Zohr, Aphrodite, and the arguments about who gets to pipe it, has turned the seabed between Egypt, Israel, and Cyprus into an energy border. TurkStream carries Russian gas to Turkey under the Black Sea. The commodity is invisible and the jurisdiction is not.

Cyber is the layer that does not need a hull. AIS, the broadcast that lets a ship be seen, can be falsified. GNSS, the signal that lets it know where it is, can be jammed or spoofed, and both have been publicly reported in the Black Sea and the Gulf since the late 2010s. Ports are industrial control systems with a waterfront. Ransomware against a terminal is a closure that looks like an IT ticket. None of this replaces the frigate. It means a closure can be partial, deniable, and cheaper than a minefield. The security buyer, a liner company or a war-risk underwriter, prices all of it as one voyage.

Displacement never left. UNHCR recorded more than 800,000 sea arrivals to Greece in 2015, the peak of a movement driven by the Syrian war and by routes through Turkey. The central Mediterranean, Libya to Italy and Malta, has been the deadlier crossing in the years since. IOM's Missing Migrants Project is the ledger of the deaths. Interdiction by coast guards, European naval missions, and Libyan forces has moved the risk without ending the demand. This is the same sea as the container sea. It is not the same legal regime. A box has a consignee. A person in a boat is treated as a problem of borders.

ports.note: The Mediterranean mouth. East Port Said is the transshipment bet beside the toll.

ports.note: Oil export and a coast where the state does not hold every pier. Departure point for people as well as barrels.

ports.name: Odessa
ports.note: The historic wheat port, struck and blockaded after 2022. The corridor is a negotiation.

ports.name: Constanta
ports.note: Romania's port takes grain and fuel the Ukrainian coast cannot ship.

ports.name: Jeddah

ports.name: Jebel Ali

commodities.name: Grain
commodities.note: Ukraine and Russia. A war premium on a food price.

commodities.name: LNG and pipeline gas
commodities.note: East Med fields, Qatari LNG, TurkStream. Energy that may never pass a port.

commodities.name: Data
commodities.note: No weight, total dependence. Cables are the commodity with no customs line.

ship.headline: The automated-enough boxship
ship.propulsion: Diesel, with a slow turn toward alternative fuels and a fast turn toward slower steaming when the rate says so
ship.navigation: GNSS, ECDIS, and a shore operations room. The ship is a node.
ship.armament: Unarmed. Security is an escort, a guard team, or a route change.
ship.note: AIS is both the safety system and the surveillance system. Turning it off is a tactic used by the shadow fleet and by anyone else who would rather not be plotted.

finance.name: War-risk premia
finance.note: Quoted by area. A Red Sea transit and a Black Sea transit became expensive, separately, after 2022 and 2023. The premium is the market's map.

finance.name: P&I clubs
finance.note: Mutual liability cover. Sanctions and dark fleets test what the club will still insure.

finance.name: Suez tolls versus the Cape
finance.note: Egypt prices the shortcut. When insurance and delay exceed the toll, the cape wins and Cairo loses the revenue.

finance.name: Port concessions
finance.note: A 30-year lease on a terminal is foreign policy conducted as infrastructure finance.

finance.name: The oil price cap
finance.note: A financial sanction enforced, or not, by insurers, banks, and the willingness of a hull to be seen.

conflicts.name: Ever Given grounding
conflicts.note: Six days. A single ship as a supply-chain halt. Not a war, and as expensive as a small one.

conflicts.name: Ukraine and the grain corridor
conflicts.note: Montreux applied. A UN grain initiative from July 2022 to July 2023. Strikes on ports before and after.

conflicts.name: Red Sea attacks
conflicts.note: Houthi attacks on commercial shipping. Diversions, escorts, and a European mission, Aspides, from 2024.

conflicts.name: Hormuz pressure
conflicts.note: Seizures, limpet mines, and the threat of closure as a negotiating position. The price moves before the strait does.

security.name: Route abandonment
security.note: The modern blockade is often a decision by a liner to stop calling. No mines required if the premium does the work.

security.name: AIS and GNSS manipulation
security.note: Publicly reported in the Black Sea and the Gulf. A ship can appear where it is not, or fail to appear at all.

security.name: Cable faults
security.note: Some are anchors and fishing gear. Some are ambiguous. Congested corridors make the difference operationally painful either way.

security.name: Port cyber risk
security.note: A terminal is a network. A ransomware event can close a gate without touching the water.

security.name: Migration interdiction
security.note: Coast guards, EU missions, and partner forces. A security regime aimed at people, running beside the regime aimed at boxes.

diplomacy.name: Montreux, applied
diplomacy.note: Turkey's 2022 closure to belligerent warships is the convention working as written. Commerce is a separate argument.

diplomacy.name: The grain initiative
diplomacy.note: A temporary treaty for food, with the UN and Turkey. It expired. The need did not.

diplomacy.name: Aspides and Prosperity Guardian
diplomacy.note: European and US-led responses to Red Sea attacks. Different mandates, overlapping water.

diplomacy.name: East Med maritime boundaries
diplomacy.note: Gas discoveries turned EEZ lines between Turkey, Greece, Cyprus, Egypt, and Israel into an energy dispute.

infrastructure.name: Transshipment hubs
infrastructure.note: Tanger Med, Piraeus, Port Said. Geography plus a concession plus a crane tall enough for the current class of ship.

infrastructure.name: The deepened canal
infrastructure.note: Egypt's new channel, opened in 2015, raised capacity and did not remove single-hull grounding risk, as 2021 showed.

infrastructure.name: Fiber landings
infrastructure.note: National decisions. The map shows corridors because the landing coordinates are someone else's asset.

infrastructure.name: LNG and gas pipes
infrastructure.note: TurkStream under the Black Sea. East Med fields behind their own maritime dispute. Fujairah's tanks outside Hormuz.

basins.name: Western Mediterranean
basins.states: Spain, France, Italy, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Gibraltar
basins.text: The economic object is the transshipment pair at Gibraltar, Tanger Med and Algeciras, plus Valencia's gateway. Politically the basin is an EU external border. Migration routes into Spain are older than the 2015 crisis and quieter than the central route. Algeria and Morocco are energy suppliers as well as neighbors, and their closure of a pipeline or a border is a European price.

basins.name: Central Mediterranean
basins.states: Italy, Malta, Libya, Tunisia
basins.text: Libya is an oil exporter with a divided coast and a departure beach for the central route. Italy is the arrival state and a naval one. Malta's flag and bunkering business is out of proportion to the island, which is the point of a flag state. The Sicily Channel is a migration corridor, a smuggling corridor, and a perfectly ordinary commercial lane, stacked.

basins.name: Adriatic and the Balkans
basins.states: Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Montenegro, Albania, Greece
basins.text: After the wars of the 1990s the Adriatic is a European coast with a memory. Container and ferry traffic is ordinary. The strategic residue is energy landing and the fact that the Balkan route of 2015 ran inland from a Greek beach. The ports are the start of a walk.

basins.name: Eastern Mediterranean
basins.states: Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Egypt
basins.text: Gas, EEZs, and the unresolved wars of the Levant. Syria's ports have been a Russian logistics interest. Lebanon's port was broken by the 2020 Beirut blast and was already a political economy of its own. Israel's terminals and Egypt's canal are the commercial constants. Turkey and Greece can be NATO allies and maritime litigants in the same week.

basins.name: Black Sea
basins.states: Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia, Georgia
basins.text: Montreux is the constitution. Russia's war closed the Ukrainian coast and made Constanta and the Danube into workarounds. Bulgaria and Romania are EU and NATO coasts on a sea they do not control. Georgia's ports are the far shore of a pipeline and a political aspiration. Insurance, not the navy, is what stops a grain ship.

basins.name: Red Sea and Suez
basins.states: Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti, Yemen
basins.text: Egypt's tolls, Jeddah's boxes, and a war in Yemen that reaches out into the shipping lane. Djibouti hosts other people's bases because the strait is narrow. Sudan and Eritrea are the coasts the route passes and the diplomacy forgets, until a civil war moves a port. The cable corridor and the ship corridor are the same water.

basins.name: Gulf and Hormuz
basins.states: Iran, Oman, UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait
basins.text: The barrel's door. Oman's Musandam and Iran face each other across the traffic lane. Fujairah exists so that some of the storage sits outside the door. Bahrain hosts a US fleet. Qatar's LNG and Saudi loading terminals assume the door stays open. Iranian pressure on shipping is a tool because the tool works on a price, not only on a hull.
